Milestone 3 Student Study Guides 
 Transfer Learning & Stronger Segmentation Models 
 Welcome to Milestone 3! In Milestone 1, you inspected raw annotations, unraveled Run-Length Encoding (RLE) memory layouts, explored line-scan sensor geometry, and studied metric sensitivity. In Milestone 2, you moved from analytical observation to active systems engineering: building custom PyTorch  Dataset  and  DataLoader  pipelines, implementing industrial geometric augmentations, establishing leakage-free validation splits, and training a baseline from-scratch U-Net. 
 In  Milestone 3 , you study stronger segmentation models through controlled experiments: 
 
 Spatial Geometry & Bottleneck Compression:  Tracing feature map dimensions through progressive stride-2 downsampling, understanding receptive field expansion, and diagnosing odd-dimension tensor parity mismatches along anisotropic ( \(128 \times 800\) ) ribbons. 
 Transfer Learning with Pretrained Vision Backbones:  Leveraging generic visual primitives (edges, gradients, textures) learned from ImageNet ( \(1.2\text{M}\)  natural images) across ResNet and EfficientNet architectures, auditing model parameters, and mastering feature-extractor freezing dynamics. 
 Grayscale Sensor Adaptation:  Solving the impedance mismatch between 3-channel RGB pretrained weights and 1-channel monochromatic industrial cameras, proving activation equivalence between channel duplication and first-layer weight collapse, and evaluating PCIe memory bandwidth efficiency. 
 Multi-Scale Context via Atrous (Dilated) Convolutions:  Analyzing DeepLabV3+ with Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) to detect both microscopic hairline cracks (1–3 pixels wide) and massive diffuse patches with wider context at a fixed feature resolution, while accounting for extra branches and sampling limitations. 
 Differentiable Soft Dice & Compound Loss Formulations:  Studying sparse-foreground objectives using smoothed Soft Dice loss ( \(\epsilon = 1.0\) ), analyzing gradient behavior on clean sheets, and anchoring training dynamics with Compound Loss ( \(\alpha \text{BCE} + \beta \text{Dice}\) ). 
 Output Head Semantics & Structural Partitioning:  Evaluating 4-channel independent Sigmoid multi-label detection against 5-channel mutually exclusive Softmax partitions, and checking representational limits under label overlap. 
 Empirical Benchmarking & Architecture Trade-offs:  Systematically measuring convergence speed, generalization gaps, parameter throughput, and memory trade-offs between scratch baselines, ResNet-34, and EfficientNet-B0.

 Every study guide corresponds directly to an assessment question in  MILESTONE_3.md . Study the core theoretical concepts, review the step-by-step diagnostic hints, and compute your results using the official starter code.

text:
Milestone 3: Transfer Learning & Stronger Segmentation Models 
 Industrial Surface Anomaly Segmentation · Milestone 3 Assessment 
 Read the  student study guides  before attempting the questions. Use the competition data in  data/public/  and compute your own results. This document contains the assessment, model/loss reference definitions and a common experiment protocol. Practice examples live in the study guides; compute assessment results yourself. 
 For Questions 8 and 9, train your models using the official starter code and standard training protocol provided below. 
 
 Overview 
 In Milestone 2, you built the data foundation: a custom PyTorch  Dataset  and  DataLoader  pipeline and trained a basic from-scratch U-Net baseline. This milestone tests whether pretrained features and alternative loss formulations help under a controlled protocol. Measure imbalance and model outcomes yourself; no fixed improvement or winning architecture is assumed. 
 Milestone 3 studies the following modeling techniques: 
 
 Encoder–Decoder Spatial Mechanics:  Feature map downsampling, bottleneck compression, skip-connection concatenation, and receptive field expansion on anisotropic ( \(128 \times 800\) ) sensor ribbons. 
 Transfer Learning with Pretrained Backbones:  Leveraging ImageNet feature hierarchies (ResNet, EfficientNet) via  segmentation_models_pytorch  (SMP), parameter audits, and fine-tuning dynamics (freeze vs. unfreeze). 
 Single-Channel Grayscale Adaptation:  Mathematically adapting 3-channel RGB pretrained weights to single-channel industrial line-scan sensors (3-channel duplication vs. first-layer weight collapse). 
 Multi-Scale Context & Atrous Convolutions:  Analyzing DeepLabV3+ with Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) to detect both fine cracks and large diffuse stains without spatial resolution collapse. 
 Compound Loss Formulations:  Replacing plain BCE with differentiable  Soft Dice Loss  and  Compound Loss ( \(\alpha \text{BCE} + \beta \text{Dice}\) )  to handle extreme foreground sparsity. 
 Output Head Semantics:  Comparing 4-channel independent Sigmoid multi-label detection with 5-channel mutually-exclusive Softmax partitions. 
 Comparative Benchmarking:  Evaluating performance gains, convergence speed, and parameter trade-offs between scratch U-Net, ResNet-34, and EfficientNet-B0. 
 
 
 🛠️ Official Starter Code & Default Parameters Reference 
 Use  segmentation-models-pytorch==0.5.0 ,  torch==2.8.0  and  torchvision==0.23.0 ; record your Python/CUDA/device versions too. In a local terminal, create a separate environment with  uv venv --python 3.11 .venv-milestone3  and install with  uv pip install --python .venv-milestone3/bin/python torch==2.8.0 torchvision==0.23.0 segmentation-models-pytorch==0.5.0 . Use the equivalent environment Python path on Windows. ImageNet weights require a download/cache; use  encoder_weights=None  for an offline  parameter audit only , not as a substitute for pretraining in Q8/Q9. 
 Use the explicit architecture settings below. All models emit raw logits. The four-pooling network in Q1 is a separate mathematical example, not this five-stage SMP encoder. 
 1. Model Instantiation & Freezing (for Questions 2, 8, 9) 
 import torch
import segmentation_models_pytorch as smp

# ResNet-34 U-Net (Model A)
model_resnet = smp.Unet(
    encoder_name="resnet34",        # Pretrained backbone
    encoder_weights="imagenet",     # Load ImageNet feature hierarchy
    in_channels=1,                  # Grayscale industrial strip
    classes=4,                      # 4 independent defect channels
    encoder_depth=5,
    decoder_channels=(256, 128, 64, 32, 16),
    decoder_use_norm="batchnorm",
    decoder_interpolation="nearest",
    activation=None
)

# EfficientNet-B0 U-Net (Model B)
model_effnet = smp.Unet(
    encoder_name="efficientnet-b0",
    encoder_weights="imagenet",
    in_channels=1,
    classes=4,
    encoder_depth=5,
    decoder_channels=(256, 128, 64, 32, 16),
    decoder_use_norm="batchnorm",
    decoder_interpolation="nearest",
    activation=None
)

# Parameter-count exercise for Q2 only; instantiate fresh unfrozen models for Q8/Q9:
for param in model_resnet.encoder.parameters():
    param.requires_grad = False 
 Setting  requires_grad=False  freezes parameters, not BatchNorm running statistics. For a deliberately fixed feature extractor, call  model.encoder.eval()  after every  model.train() . Q8/Q9 instead train all parameters with normal training-mode BatchNorm. 
 2. Differentiable Soft Dice & Compound Loss (for Questions 5, 7, 8, 9) 
 This Dice is one global ratio over the entire batch, four channels and spatial dimensions. BCE uses mean reduction. It is not a per-image/per-class Dice average. The all-empty derivation in Q7 applies to a wholly empty reduction; a clean sample in a mixed batch is coupled to other samples.
 import torch.nn as nn

class SoftDiceLoss(nn.Module):
    """Differentiable Soft Dice Loss with Laplace smoothing."""
    def __init__(self, smooth=1.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.smooth = smooth

    def forward(self, logits, targets):
        probs = torch.sigmoid(logits)
        probs_flat = probs.reshape(-1)
        targets_flat = targets.reshape(-1)
        intersection = (probs_flat * targets_flat).sum()
        dice = (2.0 * intersection + self.smooth) / (probs_flat.sum() + targets_flat.sum() + self.smooth)
        return 1.0 - dice

class CompoundLoss(nn.Module):
    """Compound Loss: alpha * BCE + beta * SoftDice."""
    def __init__(self, alpha=0.5, beta=0.5, smooth=1.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.bce = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
        self.dice = SoftDiceLoss(smooth=smooth)
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.beta = beta

    def forward(self, logits, targets):
        return self.alpha * self.bce(logits, targets) + self.beta * self.dice(logits, targets) 
 3. Common Training Protocol (for Questions 8 & 9) 
 # Standard hyperparameters for benchmarking
BATCH_SIZE = 16
LEARNING_RATE = 3e-4
WEIGHT_DECAY = 1e-2
EPOCHS = 5
ALPHA = 0.5   # BCE weight
BETA = 0.5    # Soft Dice weight
SMOOTH = 1.0  # Laplace smoothing parameter

criterion = CompoundLoss(alpha=ALPHA, beta=BETA, smooth=SMOOTH)
# For each run, first move a fresh unfrozen model to the selected device:
# model = model.to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE, weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY) 
 For Q8 compare two  ResNet-34 U-Nets of identical architecture , changing only encoder initialization ( None  versus  "imagenet" ). Match initial decoder/head state dictionaries as shown in Guide 8. Q9 compares ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-34 and EfficientNet-B0; the pretrained ResNet run may be reused. 
 Use this common protocol for all three runs: 
 
 Reuse the image-level train/validation split saved in Milestone 2, with no image ID in both partitions. Record its manifest/hash and class support. Use the same complete partitions for every model; do not use test labels or leaderboard feedback to select a result. 
 Load images as grayscale float32 in [0,1] at native height × width 128 × 800; masks are float32 binary [4,128,800] in defect_a through defect_d order. Apply no augmentations or additional mean/std normalization for this controlled baseline. This is a declared input convention, not a claim that [0,1] is optimal for pretraining. 
 Set Python, NumPy and torch seeds to 42 before each run. Reset the DataLoader generator to seed 42; use num_workers=0, shuffle=True only for training, and drop_last=False. Save sample ordering with your run metadata when possible. 
 Train all parameters, including the encoder, for exactly five epochs in float32 with fresh AdamW state, constant learning rate and no scheduler, early stopping, AMP or gradient accumulation. Use model.train() for optimization and model.eval() with inference_mode() for evaluation. Evaluate the epoch-5 model rather than selecting a best epoch. 
 Use batch size 16 for both optimization and evaluation, including the final partial batch. Report a CUDA OOM rather than silently changing one model's batch size. Use batch loss multiplied by batch image count, divided by total image count, for comparable epoch loss logs; note that the Dice term still depends on batch composition. 
 After each epoch, evaluate the train and validation partitions in eval mode without shuffling to obtain comparable loss measurements. Define the gap as |validation_eval_loss - train_eval_loss|. Record online training loss separately. 
 For hard-mask metrics, apply sigmoid followed by >=0.5 independently per defect channel, with no area filtering or threshold search. Accumulate image-class pairs over the entire validation set. 
 
 The official score is  0.70 ForegroundDice + 0.20 FalsePositiveScore + 0.10 EmptyAccuracy , using  Milestone 1 Q8's component definitions . ForegroundDice averages binary Dice only over positive target pairs; FalsePositiveScore is one minus mean predicted-positive pixel fraction on empty target pairs; EmptyAccuracy is the fraction of empty target pairs predicted entirely empty. If a denominator is missing, report it rather than fabricate a score. 
 Treat compared scalar values within absolute 1e-6 as ties. Record measured values and setup even if an observed result differs from your expectation. Hardware and library nondeterminism can prevent identical results across devices. 
 
 Question 1: Feature Map Spatial Geometry & Downsampling Arithmetic 
 In semantic segmentation, the encoder compresses input features through a series of pooling or strided convolution operations. In standard natural image segmentation (e.g.  \(256 \times 256\) ), dimensions downsample symmetrically. However, industrial line-scan strips have an extreme anisotropic aspect ratio:  \(128 \times 800\)  ( \(1:6.25\) ). 
 A semantic segmentation network processes an industrial line-scan steel strip of native shape  \((1, 128, 800)\)  across 4 progressive stride-2 downsampling stages: 
 \[\text{Input: } (128, 800) \xrightarrow{/2} \text{Stage 1: } (64, 400) \xrightarrow{/2} \text{Stage 2: } (32, 200) \xrightarrow{/2} \text{Stage 3: } (16, 100) \xrightarrow{/2} \text{Stage 4 (Bottleneck): } (H_{\text{bottle}}, W_{\text{bottle}})\] 
 Question: 
 
 What is the spatial shape  \((H_{\text{bottle}}, W_{\text{bottle}})\)  of the feature representation at the Stage 4 bottleneck? 
 If an unpadded image strip with an odd width of  \(128 \times 799\)  is passed through this 4-stage encoder with standard integer floor pooling ( kernel_size=2, stride=2 ), what is the absolute width mismatch at the  first decoder skip concatenation , immediately after doubling the Stage 4 bottleneck width and comparing it with the Stage 3 encoder skip? Assume exact 2× upsampling and no padding, cropping or interpolation-to-size before this comparison. Do not report the full-canvas reconstruction deficit. 
 What is the total spatial downsampling factor (ratio of input canvas area to bottleneck spatial area)? 
 
 Answer format:   H_bottle, W_bottle; first_skip_mismatch_px; downsample_factor 
 (Use the named fields above; example values are intentionally omitted.) 
 
 Question 2: Pretrained Backbone Architecture & Parameter Audit 
 Training a deep segmentation model from scratch on small domain datasets often struggles because early layers must learn basic visual primitives (edges, gradients, Gabor textures) from scratch. Transfer learning addresses this by using backbones pretrained on ImageNet ( \(1.2\text{M}\)  natural images). 
 Consider SMP U-Net with ResNet-34 ( encoder_name="resnet34" ) versus EfficientNet-B0 ( encoder_name="efficientnet-b0" ), both instantiated with  in_channels=1  and  classes=4  using the pinned SMP version and explicit settings in Starter Code snippet 1: 
 Question: 
 
 Compute the total parameter count (weights + biases across encoder, decoder, and segmentation head) of both models. Which architecture is more parameter-efficient, and what is the exact difference in parameter count between them? 
 In feature-extractor transfer learning, the backbone encoder is often frozen ( for p in model.encoder.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False ) while keeping the decoder and segmentation head trainable. For the ResNet-34 U-Net, what exact percentage of Model A's total parameters remain trainable? Round to 1 decimal place. 
 
 Answer format:   more_efficient_model, param_diff; trainable_pct 
 (Use the named fields above; example values are intentionally omitted.) 
 
 Question 3: Grayscale Input Adaptation (The Single-Channel Dilemma) 
 Pretrained ImageNet backbones expect 3-channel RGB inputs ( \(C_{\text{in}} = 3\) ). Industrial steel line-scan cameras produce 1-channel grayscale images ( \(C_{\text{in}} = 1\) ). 
 
 Strategy A (Channel Duplication):  Duplicate the grayscale image across 3 channels in the DataLoader ( \(X_{\text{rep}} = [I, I, I]\) ) so the 3-channel first layer ( conv1 ) can run untouched. 
 Strategy B (First-Layer Weight Collapse):  Modify the first convolutional layer ( conv1 ) to accept  \(C_{\text{in}} = 1\)  by mathematically combining the 3-channel pretrained RGB weights:  \(W_{\text{gray}} = f(W_{\text{rgb}})\) . 
 
 Assumptions:  The duplicated channels have identical values (no distinct per-channel RGB normalization), both convolutions have identical padding/stride and the bias is copied unchanged. Compare image tensor bytes only, at the same batch size, dimensions and dtype; exclude masks and downstream activations. 
 Question: 
 
 Mathematically, what exact operation  \(f(W_{\text{rgb}})\)  across the channel dimension— sum  or  mean —must be applied so that the first-layer output activations of Strategy B are strictly identical to Strategy A for any input image  \(I\) ? 
 In terms of GPU memory bandwidth and PCIe bus transfer from host to device, by what factor does Strategy B reduce the memory transfer size of the input image batch compared to Strategy A? 
 
 Answer format:   sum_or_mean, memory_factor 
 (Use the named fields above; example values are intentionally omitted.) 
 
 Question 4: Multi-Scale Receptive Fields & Atrous Convolutions (DeepLabV3+ vs. U-Net) 
 Consider fictional thin scratches and broad diffuse patches, without assigning those morphologies to competition class names. A U-Net gathers context through both convolution and downsampling, while skip connections carry higher-resolution features to the decoder. 
 DeepLabV3+ uses Atrous (Dilated) Convolutions in an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module. At fixed output size, channels and kernel size, dilation expands footprint without adding kernel parameters. Parallel ASPP branches still add computation and do not restore information already lost by downsampling.
For a  \(k \times k\)  convolutional kernel with dilation rate  \(r\) , the effective spatial footprint  \(k'\)  is given by: 
 \[k' = k + (k - 1)(r - 1)\] 
 Question: 
 
 For a standard  \(3 \times 3\)  kernel ( \(k=3\) ), what is the effective spatial footprint  \(k'\)  when the dilation rate is  \(r = 6\) , and when  \(r = 12\) ? 
 In 1–2 concise sentences: describe a potential advantage and one limitation of ASPP's multi-scale context compared with a single-scale pooling bottleneck when segmenting thin scratches and broad diffuse patches on  \(128 \times 800\)  strips. 
 
 Answer format:   k_eff_r6, k_eff_r12; brief_advantage 
 (Use the named fields above; example values are intentionally omitted.) 
 
 Question 5: Differentiable Soft Dice Loss & Numerical Smoothing 
 In an imbalanced segmentation task, background predictions can dominate pixel accuracy. BCE still penalizes missed positives; Soft Dice offers a different overlap-based objective. Use the following synthetic population for arithmetic, not as a claim about the competition distribution. 
 Consider a synthetic patch of  \(10{,}000\)  pixels containing exactly  100 defect pixels  ( \(y_i = 1\) ) and  9,900 clean background pixels  ( \(y_i = 0\) ).
Use the differentiable Soft Dice Loss formula with Laplace additive smoothing ( \(\epsilon = 1.0\) ) as defined in Starter Code snippet 2: 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}(P, Y) = 1 - \frac{2 \sum_{i=1}^N p_i y_i + \epsilon}{\sum_{i=1}^N p_i + \sum_{i=1}^N y_i + \epsilon}\] 
 Question: 
 
 Lazy Model 1:  Predicts  \(p_i = 0.01\)  uniformly across all  \(10{,}000\)  pixels. What is its exact Soft Dice Loss? 
 Accurate Model 2:  Predicts  \(p_i = 0.90\)  on all 100 defect pixels, and  \(p_i = 0.00\)  on all 9,900 background pixels. What is its exact Soft Dice Loss?
Round both answers to 4 decimal places. 
 
 Answer format:   loss_model1, loss_model2 
 (Use the named fields above; example values are intentionally omitted.) 
 
 Question 6: Output Head Semantics & Mutually Exclusive Loss Formulations 
 Recall your own pixel-level overlap audit from Milestone 1 Q3. The questions below concern the capabilities of two formulations; do not assume a training-data finding guarantees what future annotations can contain. 
 
 Formulation A (Multi-Label Sigmoid):  4 independent output channels with Sigmoid activations, trained with  BCEWithLogitsLoss . Each defect channel is predicted independently. 
 Formulation B (Multi-Class Softmax):  5 output channels (Background + 4 defect classes) with Softmax activation, trained with  CrossEntropyLoss . The network partitions each pixel into exactly one category. 
 
 Question:

 Question 7: Compound Loss Behavior on Defect vs. Clean Images 
 Modern segmentation pipelines combine BCE and Soft Dice into a Compound Loss: 
 \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Compound}} = 0.5 \times \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + 0.5 \times \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}}\] 
 Consider an entirely empty target reduction ( \(y_i=0\)  everywhere), smoothing  \(\epsilon=1\)  and probabilities  \(p_i=\sigma(z_i)\) . Let  \(S=\sum_i p_i\) . This can describe an isolated clean image or an all-clean batch, but not the contribution of a clean image in a mixed batch under the provided global Dice reduction. 
 Question:

Report both peaks in MiB and the lower-memory model ( resnet34  /  efficientnet-b0  /  tie ). Use  not_measured  on CPU-only hardware or  oom  for a model that cannot complete the specified workload. Explain why this training result alone does not establish edge inference suitability.

title: Q1 · Feature Map Geometry & Downsampling
text:
Feature Map Spatial Geometry & Downsampling Arithmetic 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 1 Study Guide) 
 1. Why Keep the Strip Geometry? 
 The competition images are height × width  \(128 \times 800\) . Resizing them to a square changes horizontal and vertical distances by different factors, which distorts defect shapes. Keep the native dimensions for this assessment. Downsampling inside a model is a separate operation: it reduces feature resolution while increasing channels and context. 
 
 This conceptual diagram illustrates skip fusion. Q1 defines its own four pooling stages; the SMP models used in Q2 use five encoder stages by default. Do not infer Q1's bottleneck from another model's diagram. 
 2. Compute Shapes from the Actual Operator 
 For dilation 1, a pooling or convolution output dimension is: 
 \[D_{out}=\left\lfloor\frac{D_{in}+2p-k}{s}\right\rfloor+1.\] 
 With  MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, ceil_mode=False) , this becomes  \(\lfloor D_{in}/2\rfloor\) . A  Conv2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1)  instead gives  \(\lceil D_{in}/2\rceil\) . They agree on even inputs but differ on odd inputs. Q1 explicitly uses the floor-pooling rule. 
 For dimensions divisible by  \(2^n\) ,  \(n\)  such pooling stages reduce each axis by  \(2^n\)  and area by  \(4^n\) . This is a sampling-area ratio,  not the receptive field : stacked convolutions can make a feature depend on a much larger input region. 
 Practice with Different Dimensions 
 Consider a fictional  \(96 \times 640\)  tensor and three pooling stages:

 The area ratio is  \((96\cdot640)/(12\cdot80)=64\) . Repeat this procedure with the assessment's dimensions and stage count yourself. 
 3. Skip Mismatch and Full-Canvas Deficit Are Different 
 A U-Net decoder concatenates a decoder tensor with an encoder skip at the same spatial resolution.  torch.cat(..., dim=1)  allows channel counts to differ, but batch, height and width must agree. 
 Use a  different toy width of 643 and three pooling stages : 
 \[643\to321\to160\to80.\] 
 Doubling the bottleneck gives 160, which matches the first skip. Doubling again gives 320, which disagrees with the next skip of width 321. A decoder with no alignment stops at that concatenation. Blindly multiplying the bottleneck by  \(2^3\)  gives 640, a full-canvas deficit of 3; that is not the mismatch at a particular skip. 
 Common alignment choices include padding the input, cropping a skip, or interpolating to the skip's explicit size: 
 import torch.nn.functional as F
# In a decoder that intentionally aligns to the skip:
upsampled = F.interpolate(decoder, size=skip.shape[-2:], mode="bilinear", align_corners=False) 
 This fixes tensor shape, not lost image detail. Q1 instead asks about the  first decoder skip , immediately after the bottleneck is doubled, before any cropping, padding or interpolation-to-size. 
 4. Practice Check 
 
 Why do the two stride-2 operators disagree at an odd width? 
 For a toy width of 101, floor pooling produces 50 while a padded 3-tap stride-2 convolution produces 51. Substituting the padding and kernel values in the general formula explains the difference. Always trace the operator used by your model.

title: Q2 · Pretrained Backbones & Parameter Audit
text:
Pretrained Backbone Architecture & Parameter Audit 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 2 Study Guide) 
 
 1. The Core Concept: The Transfer Learning Advantage 
 Training deep semantic segmentation networks from scratch can require substantial labeled data, depending on the task and architecture. On specialized industrial datasets like surface anomaly inspection, annotations are scarce, expensive to produce, and heavily skewed toward clean background material. 
 When a convolutional network is initialized randomly (e.g., via Kaiming/He normal initialization), the earliest convolutional filters possess no prior concept of visual reality. The network must learn useful image processing primitives during training: 
 
 Directional edge filters (horizontal, vertical, diagonal) 
 Color and intensity gradients 
 Local frequency and Gabor textures 
 Corner and boundary detectors 
 
 Inductive Visual Priors from ImageNet 
 Transfer learning addresses this cold-start bottleneck by utilizing feature extractors pretrained on large-scale natural image datasets such as  ImageNet-1k  ( \(1.28\text{M}\)  images across 1,000 object categories). Even though steel strips look radically different from dogs, cars, and landscapes, the  low-level physics of light, edge contrast, and spatial continuity are universal across optical sensors . 
 By adopting a pretrained encoder backbone, your model starts training with mature, robust feature hierarchies already formed: 
 
 Stages 1–2 (Shallow features):  Generic edge, ridge, and scratch primitives that transfer immediately to surface cracks. 
 Stages 3–5 (Deep features):  High-level spatial groupings that adapt rapidly to diffuse stains and structural variations. 
 
 
 2. Theoretical Principles: ResNet vs. EfficientNet Architectures 
 In modern semantic segmentation toolkits like  segmentation_models_pytorch  (SMP), a standard segmentation model decomposes into three distinct structural modules: 
 \[\text{Model} = \underbrace{\text{Encoder (Backbone)}}_{\text{Pretrained ImageNet Features}} + \underbrace{\text{Decoder}}_{\text{Feature Upsampling \& Skip Fusion}} + \underbrace{\text{Segmentation Head}}_{\text{Conv to } K \text{ Defect Classes}}\] 
 Backbone Architecture 1: ResNet-34 (Residual Networks) 
 ResNet-34 employs standard  \(3 \times 3\)  convolutional layers organized into residual blocks with additive identity shortcut connections: 
 \[\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \{W_i\}) + \mathbf{x}\] 
 The identity shortcut helps gradients propagate across deep stacks. However, standard 2D convolutions apply dense spatial-channel matrix multiplications: 
 \[\text{Parameters} = K_h \times K_w \times C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}}\] 
 For  \(3 \times 3\)  kernels across hundreds of channels, parameter counts scale quadratic with channel depth. 
 Backbone Architecture 2: EfficientNet-B0 (Compound Scaling & MBConv) 
 EfficientNet-B0 was engineered using Neural Architecture Search (NAS) and compound coefficient scaling. Instead of standard convolutions, EfficientNet utilizes  Mobile Inverted Bottleneck Convolutions (MBConv)  built from: 
 
 \(1 \times 1\)  Pointwise Expansion:  Expands channel capacity. 
 \(k \times k\)  Depthwise Convolutions:  Applies spatial filtering independently per channel ( \(C_{\text{in}} \times K_h \times K_w\)  parameters, eliminating dense cross-channel multiplying). 
 Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) Attention:  Adaptively recalibrates channel-wise feature responses. 
 \(1 \times 1\)  Pointwise Projection:  Compresses channels back down to match linear bottlenecks. 
 
 This factorization separates spatial filtering from channel mixing. Count parameters for the complete model: decoder width, expansion layers and SE blocks also contribute, and parameter savings do not guarantee equal accuracy or lower peak activation memory. 
 
 3. Parameter Accounting & Freezing Dynamics in PyTorch 
 In deep learning auditing, total parameters represent the storage footprint and parameter capacity of a model. In PyTorch, parameter tensors are queried using  model.parameters() : 
 # Total parameters (weights + biases) across all layers:
total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

# Trainable parameters (requiring gradient computation during backward pass):
trainable_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad) 
 Feature-Extractor Fine-Tuning (Encoder Freezing) 
 In the first phase of transfer learning on small datasets, it is common practice to  freeze the encoder backbone . Because ImageNet features are already well-conditioned, updating encoder weights with aggressive gradients can cause  catastrophic forgetting  (destabilizing generic edge priors). 
 By setting  requires_grad = False  on the encoder:
 for param in model.encoder.parameters():
    param.requires_grad = False 
 
 The encoder parameters no longer receive newly computed gradients. This alone does not freeze its running buffers or stochastic behavior. 
 Only the randomly initialized decoder blocks and the segmentation head receive gradient updates. 
 GPU VRAM consumption during training decreases because intermediate encoder activation gradients do not need to be retained in memory. 
 
 If a fixed feature extractor is intended, call  model.encoder.eval()   after each  model.train() . BatchNorm running mean/variance otherwise update in training mode even when its affine parameters have  requires_grad=False .  eval()  also changes dropout behavior; it does not disable gradients. Q2 asks only for parameter accounting; Q8/Q9 train all parameters with normal training-mode BatchNorm. 
 model.train()             # sets all submodules to training mode
model.encoder.eval()     # only for a deliberately fixed feature extractor 
 See  PyTorch BatchNorm2d  for the running-statistics contract and  SMP 0.5.0 model settings  for encoder/decoder options. The assessment pins SMP 0.5.0 and explicitly fixes decoder settings so parameter counts are reproducible. 
 
 This is a five-stage ResNet feature trace, separate from Q1's four-pooling toy network. Feature meanings are illustrative, not measured activations. 
 Trainable Parameter Ratio Formula 
 When the encoder is frozen, the percentage of remaining trainable parameters is: 
 \[\text{Trainable Percentage} = \frac{\sum_{p \in \text{trainable}} \text{numel}(p)}{\sum_{p \in \text{all}} \text{numel}(p)} \times 100\% = \frac{\text{Decoder Params} + \text{Head Params}}{\text{Total Model Params}} \times 100\%\] 
 
 4. Guiding Hints for Question 2 
 To solve Question 2 in  MILESTONE_3.md : 
 
 
 Hint 1 (Instantiate Models Consistently):  Instantiate both  smp.Unet  models using the exact starter code parameters:

model_resnet = smp.Unet(encoder_name="resnet34", encoder_weights="imagenet", in_channels=1, classes=4)
model_effnet = smp.Unet(encoder_name="efficientnet-b0", encoder_weights="imagenet", in_channels=1, classes=4) 
 
 
 Hint 2 (Compute Total Parameter Counts):  For both  model_resnet  and  model_effnet , write a helper function that iterates through  model.parameters()  and sums  p.numel() . Compare the two totals to determine which model is more parameter-efficient, and compute the exact numerical difference: 
 \[\Delta_{\text{params}} = |\text{params}_{\text{resnet}} - \text{params}_{\text{effnet}}|\] 
 
 
 Hint 3 (Apply Encoder Freezing):  For  model_resnet , loop over  model_resnet.encoder.parameters()  and set  param.requires_grad = False . Verify that  model_resnet.decoder  and  model_resnet.segmentation_head  parameters still have  requires_grad == True . 
 
 Hint 4 (Calculate Percentage):  Divide the count of parameters with  requires_grad == True  by the total parameter count of  model_resnet , multiply by 100, and round to 1 decimal place.

title: Q3 · Grayscale Adaptation & Channel Physics
text:
Grayscale Input Adaptation & Channel Physics 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 3 Study Guide) 
 
 1. The Core Dilemma: Monochromatic Sensors vs. Pretrained RGB Backbones 
 Every standard pretrained vision backbone on PyTorch Hub and torchvision (ResNet, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT) is configured with a 3-channel input layer: 
 \[\text{Input Tensor: } \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times H \times W} \quad (\text{Red, Green, Blue})\] 
 In high-speed manufacturing environments, optical line-scan cameras operate with monochromatic CCD or CMOS sensors. Monochromatic sensors deliver higher spatial resolution, greater dynamic range, and faster shutter speeds than Bayer-filtered color sensors because every photodiode captures full-spectrum luminescence without chromatic filtering: 
 \[\text{Industrial Strip: } \mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 1 \times H \times W} \quad (\text{Single Grayscale Intensity Channel})\] 
 This creates an immediate architectural impedance mismatch:  how do you feed a single-channel grayscale image into a neural network whose very first layer expects three input channels? 
 Two primary strategies exist in production computer vision: 
 
 Strategy A (Channel Duplication):  Replicate the grayscale image across three channels in the data pipeline. 
 Strategy B (First-Layer Weight Collapse):  Mathematically adapt the pretrained 3-channel convolutional weights to a 1-channel kernel. 
 
 
 2. Mathematical Principles: Activation Equivalence Proof 
 To evaluate the mathematical difference between Strategy A and Strategy B, let us derive the exact forward activation of the first convolutional layer ( conv1 ). 
 Let  \(\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}\)  denote an arbitrary single-channel grayscale image. Let  \(W_{\text{rgb}} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{out}} \times 3 \times k_h \times k_w}\)  denote the pretrained convolutional weights of  conv1 , which can be decomposed channel-wise into three separate sub-kernels: 
 \[W_{\text{rgb}} = [W_R, \, W_G, \, W_B]\] 
 where each  \(W_c \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{out}} \times 1 \times k_h \times k_w}\)  represents the filter weights acting on the Red, Green, and Blue channels respectively, with shared bias vector  \(\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{out}}}\) . 
 Strategy A: Channel Duplication 
 In Strategy A, the DataLoader duplicates the single grayscale image across all three channels: 
 \[\mathbf{X}_{\text{rep}} = [\mathbf{I}, \, \mathbf{I}, \, \mathbf{I}] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}\] 
 Passing  \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{rep}}\)  through the original 3-channel convolution yields the output feature map  \(\mathbf{Y}_A\) : 
 \[\mathbf{Y}_A = W_{\text{rgb}} \ast \mathbf{X}_{\text{rep}} + \mathbf{b} = (W_R \ast \mathbf{I}) + (W_G \ast \mathbf{I}) + (W_B \ast \mathbf{I}) + \mathbf{b}\] 
 By the distributive property of 2D cross-correlation (convolution): 
 \[\mathbf{Y}_A = \big(W_R + W_G + W_B\big) \ast \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{b} = \left(\sum_{c \in \{R, G, B\}} W_c \right) \ast \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{b}\] 
 Strategy B: First-Layer Weight Collapse 
 In Strategy B, we modify  conv1  so its input channels  \(C_{\text{in}} = 1\) . The new weight tensor is  \(W_{\text{gray}} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\text{out}} \times 1 \times k_h \times k_w}\) . Passing the single-channel image  \(\mathbf{I}\)  through this layer yields: 
 \[\mathbf{Y}_B = W_{\text{gray}} \ast \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{b}\] 
 The Strict Activation Equivalence Condition 
 For Strategy B to produce  strictly identical  feature representations to Strategy A for every possible input image ( \(\mathbf{Y}_B \equiv \mathbf{Y}_A \ \forall \ \mathbf{I}\) ): 
 \[W_{\text{gray}} \ast \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{b} \equiv \left(\sum_{c \in \{R, G, B\}} W_c \right) \ast \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{b}\] 
 \[W_{\text{gray}} = \sum_{c \in \{R, G, B\}} W_c = \text{sum}\big(W_{\text{rgb}}, \, \text{dim}=1\big)\] 
 Why the Channel Mean Fails Equivalence 
 A common beginner trap is computing the channel-wise average: 
 \[W_{\text{mean}} = \frac{1}{3} \big(W_R + W_G + W_B\big)\] 
 If you use the mean, the output activation is: 
 \[\mathbf{Y}_{\text{mean}} = \frac{\mathbf{Y}_A-\mathbf{b}}{3}+\mathbf{b}.\] 
 The convolution contribution is scaled by one third; the copied bias is unchanged. Only with zero bias does the entire output equal  \(\mathbf{Y}_A/3\) . A changed scale can affect a downstream BatchNorm using pretrained running statistics; its effect after fine-tuning must be measured. The equivalence proof assumes identical channel inputs, padding and copied biases. Separate RGB mean/std normalization after duplication generally makes the channels unequal and breaks that assumption. 
 In PyTorch  segmentation_models_pytorch , passing  in_channels=1  automatically implements Strategy B using  channel summation :
 # SMP internal implementation when in_channels=1:
new_weight = pretrained_weight.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
model.encoder.conv1.weight.data = new_weight 
 
 
 These are alternative input strategies. The weight-combination rule and normalization assumptions must be stated explicitly; an average and a sum are not activation-equivalent. 
 3. Hardware & Memory Bandwidth: Host-to-Device (PCIe) Transfer 
 Beyond mathematical equivalence, input channel selection has direct implications for training throughput and hardware resource consumption. 
 In modern deep learning training workflows: 
 
 Data augmentations and preprocessing run on the host CPU. 
 Batches are transferred from host RAM across the  PCIe bus  (e.g., PCIe 4.0 x16 at ~31.5 GB/s) to GPU VRAM via  batch.to(device) . 
 The forward and backward passes execute on the GPU Tensor Cores. 
 
 Host CPU (RAM) ──────── PCIe Bus Transfer ────────► GPU Device (VRAM)
Strategy A: [B, 3, 128, 800] (Float32: 3 × 400 KB = 1.2 MB / strip)
Strategy B: [B, 1, 128, 800] (Float32: 1 × 400 KB = 0.4 MB / strip)  <--- 3x Less Data! 
 Memory Bandwidth Scaling Factor 
 Let  \(B\)  be the batch size, and  \((H, W) = (128, 800)\) . For 32-bit floating-point tensors ( torch.float32 , 4 bytes per element): 
 
 
 Strategy A Batch Size in Bytes: 
 \[\text{Bytes}_A = B \times 3 \times 128 \times 800 \times 4\text{ bytes} = B \times 1{,}228{,}800\text{ bytes}\] 
 
 
 Strategy B Batch Size in Bytes: 
 \[\text{Bytes}_B = B \times 1 \times 128 \times 800 \times 4\text{ bytes} = B \times 409{,}600\text{ bytes}\] 
 
 
 \[\text{Transfer Reduction Factor} = \frac{\text{Bytes}_A}{\text{Bytes}_B} = \frac{3}{1} = 3\times\] 
 Strategy B reduces the volume of image data transferred across the PCIe bus by an exact factor of  \(3\times\)  (a  \(66.7\%\)  reduction). On multi-GPU distributed clusters or bandwidth-constrained systems, this reduces input-transfer bytes, but does not guarantee that I/O is the bottleneck or that total peak VRAM falls by the same factor. Downstream activations, optimizer state and device-side repetition also matter. 
 
 4. Guiding Hints for Question 3 
 To solve Question 3 in  MILESTONE_3.md : 
 
 Hint 1 (Recall Cross-Correlation Linearity):  Re-read the derivation in Section 2 above. Convolution is a linear operator:  \(W \ast X = \sum_c W_c \ast X_c\) . When  \(X_0 = X_1 = X_2 = I\) , the three operations combine into a single convolution by summing the kernel weights. Choose between  sum  and  mean . 
 
 Hint 2 (Verify in PyTorch):  You can verify this identity empirically in PyTorch on CPU:

import torch.nn as nn

conv_rgb = nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, bias=True)
conv_gray = nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=3, bias=True)
conv_gray.weight.data = conv_rgb.weight.data.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
conv_gray.bias.data = conv_rgb.bias.data

x_gray = torch.randn(2, 1, 128, 800)
x_rgb = x_gray.repeat(1, 3, 1, 1)

diff = (conv_rgb(x_rgb) - conv_gray(x_gray)).abs().max().item()
print("Max absolute difference:", diff)  # small floating-point rounding differences are expected
torch.testing.assert_close(conv_rgb(x_rgb), conv_gray(x_gray), rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6) 
 
 
 Hint 3 (Compute Memory Factor):  Determine the ratio of input tensor elements between a 3-channel batch  [B, 3, 128, 800]  and a 1-channel batch  [B, 1, 128, 800] . Express the reduction factor in the standard multiplier format (e.g.,  2x  or  3x ). 
 
 
 
 5. Your Assignment Task

title: Q4 · Atrous Convolutions & ASPP
text:
Multi-Scale Receptive Fields & Atrous Convolutions 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 4 Study Guide) 
 
 1. The Engineering Dilemma: Hairline Cracks vs. Massive Diffuse Patches 
 In industrial surface defect inspection, anomalies exhibit extreme scale divergence across classes: 
 
 Fictional thin scratch:  High-frequency, sub-millimeter cracks that are only  1 to 3 pixels wide , requiring precise sub-pixel boundary localization. 
 Fictional diffuse patch:  Low-frequency, sprawling textures that span  hundreds of pixels  across the  \(128 \times 800\)  steel ribbon, requiring extensive contextual awareness to distinguish subtle discolored sheen from normal surface reflection. 
 
 In a U-Net, both stacked convolutions and spatial downsampling expand the receptive field. Skip connections carry higher-resolution features around the bottleneck. Atrous convolution offers another way to gather wider context without another downsampling operation. 
 The Traditional Downsampling Paradox:
Input (128x800) ──► Pooling (32x) ──► Receptive field is large enough for Defect C,
                                       BUT spatial resolution drops to (4x25).
                                       Fine boundaries may become harder to localize from this coarse tensor alone. 
 If you do not downsample, the receptive field of standard  \(3 \times 3\)  convolutions grows linearly and slowly: 
 \[\text{Receptive Field} = 1 + L \times (k - 1)\] 
 To achieve a receptive field of 100 pixels with standard  \(3 \times 3\)  convolutions without downsampling, you would need 50 stacked convolutional layers, which can be expensive; actual latency and optimization depend on the implementation. 
 
 2. Mathematical Principles: Atrous (Dilated) Convolutions 
 To break this fundamental trade-off between  receptive field size  and  spatial resolution , Chen et al. introduced  Atrous (Dilated) Convolutions  in the DeepLab family of architectures ( atrous  is derived from the French  à trous , meaning "with holes"). 
 An atrous convolution introduces a  dilation rate  \(r\)  into standard 2D convolution: 
 
 When  \(r = 1\) , the convolution is a standard dense convolution with adjacent kernel taps. 
 When  \(r > 1\) , the kernel expands its spatial footprint by inserting  \(r - 1\)  spaces ("holes") between consecutive filter weights along each spatial axis. 
 
 1D Visual Schematic of Kernel Dilation (k=3):
r = 1 (Standard):    [ W0 ] [ W1 ] [ W2 ]                 Footprint = 3 pixels
r = 2 (Dilation=2):  [ W0 ]   ·   [ W1 ]   ·   [ W2 ]     Footprint = 5 pixels
r = 3 (Dilation=3):  [ W0 ]   ·     ·   [ W1 ]   ·     ·   [ W2 ] Footprint = 7 pixels 
 Derivation of the Effective Spatial Footprint ( \(k'\) ) 
 Consider a 1D or 2D convolutional filter with kernel size  \(k\)  and dilation rate  \(r\) : 
 
 The kernel contains  \(k\)  active weight coefficients along an axis. 
 Between the  \(k\)  weights, there are  \((k - 1)\)  intervals. 
 In a standard convolution ( \(r=1\) ), each interval spans 1 pixel step. 
 When dilated by rate  \(r\) , each interval spans  \(r\)  pixel steps. 
 Therefore, the distance from the first weight to the last weight is  \((k - 1) \times r\)  steps. 
 Including the initial anchor pixel, the total effective spatial footprint  \(k'\)  covered by the kernel is: 
 
 \[k' = 1 + (k - 1) \times r = k + (k - 1)(r - 1)\] 
 Let us verify this formula: 
 
 If  \(r = 1\) :  \(k' = k + (k - 1)(0) = k\)  (standard kernel footprint). 
 If  \(k = 3, r = 2\) :  \(k' = 3 + (3 - 1)(2 - 1) = 3 + 2 = 5\) . 
 If  \(k = 3, r = 3\) :  \(k' = 3 + (3 - 1)(3 - 1) = 3 + 4 = 7\) . 
 
 Parameter Count at Fixed Feature Resolution 
 For equal input/output channels, groups, kernel size and  output feature dimensions , changing dilation leaves the parameter count and nominal MAC count unchanged. Appropriate padding is needed to preserve output dimensions. Actual latency can differ, and parallel ASPP branches add work compared with one branch. 
 
 A standard  \(3 \times 3\)  kernel contains  \(3 \times 3 = 9\)  weights. 
 A toy dilated  \(3 \times 3\)  kernel with  \(r = 4\)  has a  \(9 \times 9\)  footprint, but still samples  9 locations per input/output channel pair . 
 A dense  \(9 \times 9\)  kernel samples 81 locations per channel pair. The dilated kernel spans the same extent but does not inspect every location; sparse sampling can miss small structures. 
 
 
 3. DeepLabV3+ & Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) 
 Rather than choosing a single dilation rate,  DeepLabV3+  captures multi-scale context simultaneously using an  Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP)  module placed at the encoder bottleneck. 
 DeepLabV3+ ASPP Architecture:
Bottleneck Features [C_in, H, W]
       │
       ├──► 1x1 Conv (r=1)                     ──────────► [C_out, H, W] (Local feature mixing)
       ├──► 3x3 Dilated Conv (r=6)             ──────────► [C_out, H, W] (Intermediate scratch context)
       ├──► 3x3 Dilated Conv (r=12)            ──────────► [C_out, H, W] (Large diffuse defect context)
       ├──► 3x3 Dilated Conv (r=18)            ──────────► [C_out, H, W] (Global ribbon context)
       └──► Global Average Pooling + 1x1 Conv  ──────────► [C_out, H, W] (Canvas-level scene prior)
                                                                 │
                                                   Concat all 5 branches
                                                                 │
                                                       1x1 Projection Conv
                                                                 ▼
                                                  Multi-Scale Fused Representation 
 What ASPP Adds to a Bottleneck 
 
 Parallel Multi-Scale Processing:  Instead of forcing all features through a single bottleneck scale, ASPP queries the feature representation at multiple sampling rates in parallel. 
 Preservation of Fine Details:  Small-dilation branches sample nearby features. They cannot recover fine information already lost in the encoder; DeepLabV3+ also uses lower-level features in its decoder. 
 Macroscopic Texture Aggregation:  Larger dilation branches sample farther-apart features. Their useful context depends on output stride, feature size and padding; on short strips some taps may fall outside the feature map. 
 Resolution Retention:  The entire operation is performed without further spatial downsampling inside ASPP. This alone does not guarantee better boundaries or scores. 
 
 
 4. Guiding Hints for Question 4 
 To solve Question 4 in  MILESTONE_3.md : 
 
 
 Hint 1 (Apply the Footprint Formula):  Use the derived footprint formula: 
 \[k' = k + (k - 1)(r - 1)\] 
 For a standard  \(3 \times 3\)  kernel ( \(k=3\) ): 
 
 Substitute  \(r = 6\)  to find  \(k'_{\text{r6}}\) . 
 Substitute  \(r = 12\)  to find  \(k'_{\text{r12}}\) . 
 Express your answers as 2D spatial dimensions:  k'xk' ; calculate both numbers yourself. 
 Hint 2 (Formulate the Architectural Advantage):  In 1 to 2 concise sentences, describe the potential benefit and one limitation of ASPP compared with a single-scale pooling bottleneck. Your sentence should mention: 
 Capturing  multi-scale context  across diverse anomaly scales (microscopic cracks vs. large patches). 
 Preserving  spatial feature resolution  without aggressive downsampling. 
 
 
 
 
 5. Your Assignment Task

title: Q5 · Soft Dice Loss & Laplace Smoothing
text:
Differentiable Soft Dice Loss & Numerical Smoothing 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 5 Study Guide) 
 1. Sparse Foreground and the Objective 
 A model can attain high pixel accuracy on a sparse-defect dataset by predicting background too often. This does not make all-background prediction the mathematical optimum of BCE: a missed positive pixel still has a nonzero logit gradient. At an exactly zero predicted probability on a positive target, ideal BCE is unbounded. The practical concern is imbalance in aggregate contributions and shared-parameter updates, not an absence of a foreground penalty. 
 Measure class and pixel distributions yourself. This guide's numerical examples are fictional and reveal no competition statistics. 
 2. From Hard Overlap to a Differentiable Loss 
 Binary Dice compares a predicted set  \(X\)  and target set  \(Y\) : 
 \[D(X,Y)=\frac{2|X\cap Y|}{|X|+|Y|}.\] 
 Thresholding probabilities creates a step function, so hard Dice is unsuitable as a direct differentiable training loss. In the assessment's Soft Dice, use probabilities  \(p_i=\sigma(z_i)\) : 
 \[L_D=1-\frac{2\sum_i p_i y_i+\epsilon}{\sum_i p_i+\sum_i y_i+\epsilon}.\] 
 Compute three quantities before substituting: intersection  \(I=\sum p_i y_i\) , predicted mass  \(P=\sum p_i\) , and target mass  \(T=\sum y_i\) . Then  \(L_D=1-(2I+\epsilon)/(P+T+\epsilon)\) . 
 Reduction matters.  The supplied  SoftDiceLoss  flattens all batch, channel and spatial dimensions into one global ratio. It is not an average of per-image or per-class Dice losses. Document that reduction when comparing implementations; a clean image inside a mixed batch is coupled to positives elsewhere in the batch. 
 3. What Smoothing Changes 
 With  \(\epsilon>0\) , an entirely empty reduction ( \(P=T=0\) ) gives Dice 1 and loss 0. Without smoothing the ratio is undefined. Smoothing also changes losses and gradients for small objects; its numerical value is part of the objective, not just a harmless implementation detail. 
 Smoothing does not guarantee stable optimization under every probability distribution. Read  Guide 7  to distinguish the value of a loss from its gradient. 
 
 These are synthetic probability sweeps, not training results. The first two panels use different y-axis scales for BCE and Dice, so compare trends rather than line heights. A steep-looking loss curve does not establish a steep logit gradient. 
 4. Worked Practice with Different Inputs 
 Use a fictional  20-pixel patch with 4 positives , smoothing  \(\epsilon=1\) . 
 Model U  predicts 0.2 at every pixel. Then  \(I=4\cdot0.2=0.8\) ,  \(P=20\cdot0.2=4\) , and  \(T=4\) . Thus: 
 \[L_D=1-\frac{2(0.8)+1}{4+4+1}=1-\frac{2.6}{9}\approx0.7111.\] 
 Model V  predicts 0.75 at the four positives and 0.05 at the sixteen negatives. Then  \(I=3\) ,  \(P=3+0.8=3.8\) , and  \(T=4\) : 
 \[L_D=1-\frac{2(3)+1}{3.8+4+1}=1-\frac{7}{8.8}\approx0.2045.\] 
 Even small background probabilities contribute to  \(P\) . Foreground confidence contributes both to  \(P\)  and to the overlap numerator. This explains the distinct effects of missed foreground and background leakage. 
 
 Practice: Model V now predicts zero on background. How does the loss change? 
 Now  \(P=3\) ,  \(I=3\) ,  \(T=4\) , so  \(L_D=1-7/8=0.125\) . Removing background leakage improves overlap without changing foreground confidence. These practice values differ from the assessment. 
 
 5. Verify the Practice Calculation

p = torch.full((20,), 0.2, dtype=torch.float64)
y = torch.zeros_like(p)
y[:4] = 1
loss = 1 - (2 * (p * y).sum() + 1) / (p.sum() + y.sum() + 1)
print(float(loss))

title: Q6 · Output Heads & Target Semantics
text:
Output Head Semantics & Loss Formulations 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 6 Study Guide) 
 
 1. The Core Architectural Choice: Sigmoid vs. Softmax 
 When configuring the final output layer of a semantic segmentation model, deep learning practitioners face a foundational design choice: 
                ┌──► Formulation A: 4-Channel Independent Sigmoid (Multi-Label)
Decoder Logits │    Shape: [B, 4, H, W]  │  Trained with BCEWithLogitsLoss
               │
               └──► Formulation B: 5-Channel Mutually Exclusive Softmax (Multi-Class)
                    Shape: [B, 5, H, W]  │  Trained with CrossEntropyLoss 
 This choice governs not only the loss function and activation mathematics, but also the fundamental representational capacity of your inspection system. 
 
 2. Mathematical Principles: Activation & Target Semantics 
 Formulation A: 4-Channel Independent Sigmoid 
 In Formulation A, the network outputs 4 continuous logit feature maps matching the 4 defect classes ( defect_a ,  defect_b ,  defect_c ,  defect_d ): 
 \[\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 4 \times H \times W}\] 
 Each channel is passed through an independent Sigmoid function: 
 \[P_c(y, x) = \sigma\big(z_c(y, x)\big) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z_c(y, x)}} \in [0, 1]\] 
 
 Target Representation:  Dense binary floating-point tensor of shape  [B, 4, H, W] . 
 Loss Function:   nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()  computed independently across all 4 channels and all pixels. 
 Semantic Freedom:  Changing one output logit does not change another channel's sigmoid value; shared network parameters can still couple training updates. A pixel  \((y, x)\)  can simultaneously have high probabilities for multiple defect categories (e.g.,  \(P_a(y, x) = 0.92\)  and  \(P_c(y, x) = 0.88\) ). If all four channels are below the decision threshold ( \(P_c < \tau\) ), the pixel is implicitly classified as background. 
 
 Formulation B: 5-Channel Mutually Exclusive Softmax 
 In Formulation B, an explicit  Background Class (Channel 0)  is added, creating 5 total output channels: 
 \[\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 5 \times H \times W} \quad (\text{0: Background, 1: Defect A, 2: Defect B, 3: Defect C, 4: Defect D})\] 
 Probabilities are computed via the Softmax operator across the channel dimension at every spatial coordinate  \((y, x)\) : 
 \[P_c(y, x) = \frac{e^{z_c(y, x)}}{\sum_{k=0}^4 e^{z_k(y, x)}}\] 
 
 Target Representation:  2D integer class index map of shape  [B, H, W]  where each pixel holds an integer class label  \(Y(y, x) \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\) . 
 Loss Function:   nn.CrossEntropyLoss() . 
 
 Probability Simplex Constraint:  At every single pixel coordinate  \((y, x)\) , the channel probabilities strictly sum to 1: 
 \[\sum_{c=0}^4 P_c(y, x) = 1.0\] 
 If one class probability increases, the sum of the remaining probabilities must decrease. If only that class logit is increased while other logits stay fixed, each other probability decreases; under arbitrary simultaneous logit changes, some other individual probabilities may still increase. 
 
 
 
 3. Spatial Disjointness vs. Pixel-Level Overlap 
 Use your own Milestone 1 Q3 overlap audit to decide whether a mutually exclusive target map preserves all observed labels. Image-level co-occurrence alone does not answer that question. A finding on the training set also does not guarantee that future annotations have the same property. 
 
 This single-pixel toy example illustrates activation rules, not an empirical finding about the competition data. 
 Can Softmax Segment Multiple Defects on the Same Sheet? 
 A frequent misconception is that Softmax restricts a model to predicting only one defect class per image.  This is false. 
 
 Softmax is applied  independently at each spatial pixel  \((y, x)\) . 
 
 At pixel  \((y, x) = (50, 100)\)  on the left side of the sheet, the model can predict: 
 \[P_{\text{defect\_a}}(50, 100) = 0.95, \quad P_{\text{bg}} = 0.04, \quad P_{\text{others}} \approx 0.01\] 
 
 
 At pixel  \((y, x) = (50, 700)\)  on the right side of the sheet, the model can independently predict: 
 \[P_{\text{defect\_c}}(50, 700) = 0.94, \quad P_{\text{bg}} = 0.05, \quad P_{\text{others}} \approx 0.01\] 
 
 
 Because spatial coordinates are decoupled, Formulation B can cleanly segment multiple defect instances across disjoint regions of the same steel sheet without mutual interference. 
 The Operational Failure Mode of Formulation B 
 However, Formulation B has a critical operational vulnerability:  it fundamentally cannot represent overlapping annotations at the same spatial pixel . 
 The Overlap Breakdown:
Suppose a hairline scratch (Defect A) cuts across a large oxide inclusion (Defect C) at pixel (y, x):
- True physical reality: Both Defect A and Defect C are present simultaneously.
- Integer Class Target: Target tensor must choose ONE integer: y(y, x) = 1 OR y(y, x) = 3.
                        Whichever defect is omitted is treated as FALSE (loss penalizes it!).
- Softmax Probabilities: sum(P_c) = 1.0. If P_A = 0.8, P_C CANNOT exceed 0.2! 
 With an integer class target and argmax prediction, an overlapping pixel must be assigned only one class, so at least one true label is lost there. This is a representational limitation at overlapping pixels; it does not imply failure across an entire image. Softmax probabilities alone do not force argmax decoding, but this particular single-label formulation does. 
 
 4. Comparative Decision Matrix 
 
 
 
 Dimension 
 Formulation A (4-Ch Sigmoid) 
 Formulation B (5-Ch Softmax) 
 
 
 
 
 Output Activation 
 Channel-wise Sigmoid  \(\sigma(z_c) \in [0, 1]\) 
 Cross-channel Softmax  \(\sum P_c = 1.0\)

 CrossEntropyLoss

 Long  [B, 128, 800]  (integers 0..4)

 Fully supported 
 Fully supported

 Fully supported (each channel independent) 
 Cannot preserve multiple labels with a single integer/argmax output

 Explicit (dedicated Channel 0) 
 
 
 
 
 5. Guiding Hints for Question 6 
 To solve Question 6 in  MILESTONE_3.md : 
 
 Hint 1 (Spatially Separated Defects):  Consider whether Softmax normalization is computed across spatial coordinates or across the channel depth at each individual coordinate  \((y, x)\) . Since Softmax operates per-pixel, can the left half of an image predict class A while the right half predicts class C? Choose  Yes  or  No . 
 Hint 2 (Failure Mode Under Overlap):  In 1 concise sentence, identify why Formulation B fails if defects overlap at the exact same pixel  \((y, x)\) . Note that integer target representation and the Softmax probability simplex ( \(\sum P_c = 1\) ) force mutual exclusivity at the pixel level, preventing a single pixel from being classified into multiple categories simultaneously. 
 
 
 6. Your Assignment Task

title: Q7 · Compound Loss & Clean Image Dynamics
text:
Compound Loss Behavior on Defect vs. Clean Images 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 7 Study Guide) 
 1. Why Compare BCE and Dice? 
 BCE supplies local pixel-wise classification signals; Soft Dice couples pixels through an overlap ratio. A weighted sum can balance these signals, but its performance depends on reduction, weights, data and optimization. It is a hypothesis to test, not a theorem that the combination always wins. 
 The assessment fixes: 
 \[L=0.5L_{BCE}+0.5L_D.\] 
 Pass raw logits to  BCEWithLogitsLoss  and to the provided  SoftDiceLoss . The latter applies sigmoid internally. Do not threshold predictions during training. 
 2. Define the Reduction Before Discussing a Clean Image 
 The starter's Dice flattens the  entire batch and all four channels . The following all-empty derivation applies when every target in that reduction is zero, or when Dice is deliberately computed on one isolated clean image. It does not describe a clean sample's contribution inside a mixed positive/clean batch: positives elsewhere affect that sample's numerator and denominator derivatives. 
 Let  \(S=\sum_i p_i\) , and let all  \(y_i=0\) . With smoothing  \(\epsilon\) : 
 \[L_D=1-\frac{\epsilon}{S+\epsilon}=\frac{S}{S+\epsilon}.\] 
 The loss is zero at  \(S=0\)  and approaches one as predicted mass grows. For a  toy mass of 9  with  \(\epsilon=1\) , the loss is  \(9/10=0.9\) . This is a large loss value; it says nothing by itself about the size of a parameter update. 
 3. Follow the Derivative through Sigmoid 
 For a probability  \(p_j\) : 
 \[\frac{\partial L_D}{\partial p_j}=\frac{\epsilon}{(S+\epsilon)^2}.\] 
 For its logit  \(z_j\) , the sigmoid chain rule gives: 
 \[\frac{\partial L_D}{\partial z_j}=\frac{\epsilon p_j(1-p_j)}{(S+\epsilon)^2}.\] 
 As total mass increases, the shared denominator grows. A saturated positive probability also makes  \(p_j(1-p_j)\)  small. Consequently a nearly maximal loss can coexist with weak logit gradients. For the toy mass  \(S=9\) ,  \(\epsilon=1\)  and  \(p_j=0.5\) , the logit derivative is  \(0.25/100=0.0025\) . 
 As all probabilities approach zero, the probability derivative approaches  \(1/\epsilon\) , whereas the  logit derivative  approaches zero through the sigmoid factor. There is no positive noise threshold where this differentiable loss stops working: for finite logits and positive smoothing, its all-empty logit derivative remains positive, though floating-point saturation can produce numerical zeros. 
 4. How BCE Contributes 
 With mean reduction over  \(N\)  elements: 
 \[\frac{\partial L_{BCE}}{\partial z_j}=\frac{p_j-y_j}{N}.\] 
 On a clean target this is  \(p_j/N\) . It does not contain Dice's shared probability-mass denominator or sigmoid derivative factor. A confidently wrong background prediction therefore still receives a BCE logit signal. Near  \(p_j=0\) , BCE's signal also tends toward zero; it is not a promise of permanent margin enforcement. 
 BCE is convex as a function of individual logits, but a neural network trained with it is not generally convex in its parameters. The relative size of the BCE/Dice contributions depends on  \(N\) , smoothing and reduction. Compare gradients or controlled validation runs rather than assuming equal coefficients imply equal effects. 
 5. A Small Autograd Check 
 import torch
z = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
p = z.sigmoid()
eps = 1.0
loss = 1 - eps / (p.sum() + eps)  # all-zero target
loss.backward()
expected = eps * p.detach() * (1 - p.detach()) / (p.detach().sum() + eps)**2
torch.testing.assert_close(z.grad, expected)
print(z.grad) 
 
 Practice: Is a high Dice loss evidence of exploding gradients? 
 No. The scalar loss and its derivative answer different questions. Inspect the derivative with respect to the quantity actually optimized: logits are further transformed through network parameters. The all-empty formula above shows why a large predicted mass can raise loss while suppressing the logit gradient. 
 
 6. Guiding Hints and Assignment Task

Explain what signal BCE adds and one limitation of claiming the combination must always outperform Dice alone. State whether your argument concerns an all-empty reduction or a mixed batch.

title: Q8 · Scratch vs. Pretrained Convergence
text:
Scratch Baseline vs. Pretrained Transfer Learning 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 8 Study Guide) 
 1. Ask a Question the Experiment Can Answer 
 Pretraining can supply useful visual features, but a domain shift, different normalization or a short training budget can change the outcome. Faster convergence, a smaller generalization gap and a higher score are  hypotheses to measure . There is no predetermined winner or score-improvement band. 
 For Q8, compare the  same SMP ResNet-34 U-Net architecture  with random versus ImageNet encoder initialization. This isolates encoder initialization; comparing a different basic U-Net from Milestone 2 would also change architecture and would not isolate pretraining. 
 A useful experiment matrix has one row per run and columns for initialization, backbone, split, seed, loss, training settings and evaluation rules. Mark the one column allowed to change before training. This prevents accidental changes such as freezing only one model or applying a threshold sweep to only one result. 
 2. Fix the Protocol Before Looking at Results 
 Use the  assessment protocol : the same saved split, image preprocessing, augmentation policy, sample order, batch size, optimizer, epochs and metric. The assessment fixes native single-channel [0,1] input, no augmentations, full precision, all parameters trainable, normal training-mode BatchNorm, and threshold 0.5 with no area filter. Q2's frozen encoder is a parameter-count exercise, not the training configuration for Q8. 
 import torch
import segmentation_models_pytorch as smp

def make_model(weights):
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    return smp.Unet(
        encoder_name="resnet34", encoder_weights=weights,
        encoder_depth=5, decoder_channels=(256, 128, 64, 32, 16),
        decoder_use_norm="batchnorm", decoder_interpolation="nearest",
        in_channels=1, classes=4, activation=None,
    )

scratch = make_model(None)
pretrained = make_model("imagenet")
# Match decoder/head initialization explicitly to remove another source of variation.
pretrained.decoder.load_state_dict(scratch.decoder.state_dict())
pretrained.segmentation_head.load_state_dict(scratch.segmentation_head.state_dict()) 
 Train one model at a time with a fresh optimizer. Reset the data-order generator and RNGs before each run. Do not reuse optimizer state or carry forward the Q2 freeze. Record library versions and the saved split; GPU kernels can still introduce small run-to-run differences. 
 3. Use the Official Weighted Metric 
 Follow  Milestone 1 Q8's definitions : 
 \[Score=0.70\,ForegroundDice+0.20\,FalsePositiveScore+0.10\,EmptyAccuracy.\] 
 
 ForegroundDice:  mean binary Dice over image-class pairs with a nonempty target. 
 FalsePositiveScore:  one minus mean predicted-positive pixel fraction over ground-truth empty image-class pairs. 
 EmptyAccuracy:  fraction of ground-truth empty pairs predicted completely empty. 
 
 Accumulate these components over the  whole validation set , not equally over uneven batches. Check that the split contains positive and empty pairs; report a missing denominator rather than inventing a score. Do not substitute average Dice over all pairs or Soft Dice training loss for this weighted metric. 
 Use sigmoid followed by  >= 0.5  on every channel, with no connected-component filtering for this comparison. Compute the official score and foreground Dice from those binary masks. 
 4. Read Learning Curves without Predicting Their Outcome 
 At epochs 1 and 5 record foreground Dice, official score and validation loss. A higher score and lower loss need not select the same model: they measure different properties. Report the two winners separately, including ties. 
 For the generalization comparison, evaluate  both the training split and validation split in eval mode  after the epoch, without augmentation. Average loss using the same fixed batch size and sample-weighted batch aggregation on both splits. This avoids comparing online training losses (collected while weights change and BatchNorm uses batch statistics) directly with an eval-mode loss. The Dice term is batch-coupled, so record the batching as well. 
 Compute: 
 \[G=|L_{val,eval}-L_{train,eval}|.\] 
 A smaller gap alone does not prove a better model: an underfit model can be equally poor on both sets. Read the gap alongside validation quality. 
 5. Worked Practice on Fictional Logs 
 Suppose a toy experiment gives model R score 0.41 and model S score 0.40. Then  \(\Delta Score=0.01\)  for R minus S. If R's train/validation eval losses are 0.30/0.34, its gap is 0.04. If S's are 0.33/0.35, its gap is 0.02. R has the better score but S has the tighter gap. These invented logs do not predict the assessment's outcome. 
 6. Guiding Hints and Assignment Task 
 Read  Question 8 . Keep a small per-epoch table containing model, seed, split ID, eval losses, foreground Dice and all three score components. At epoch 5 compute pretrained score minus scratch score, then choose the exhaustive band listed in the question. 
 Report the measured loss winner, score winner, epoch-1 foreground-Dice winner, gap comparison and signed score difference. Unexpected results are valid when your setup and measurements are documented. Do not select an answer based on a theoretical expectation.

title: Q9 · Backbone Architecture Trade-offs
text:
Pretrained Backbone Architecture Trade-off 
 (Milestone 3 · Question 9 Study Guide) 
 1. Separate Capacity, Memory and Accuracy 
 Model selection involves several different quantities: parameter storage, activation memory, training optimizer state, latency and validation quality. A lower parameter count proves a smaller parameter tensor budget at the same dtype; it does not prove lower peak VRAM, faster inference or better segmentation. 
 For Q9 compare ImageNet-initialized ResNet-34 and EfficientNet-B0 U-Nets under the  same five-epoch protocol . Change the encoder architecture, keeping the decoder settings and training/evaluation rules fixed. This compares the two complete recipes, not a universal ranking of backbone families. 
 2. Audit Parameters Yourself 
 Use Q2's counts for the complete model, including encoder, decoder and segmentation head: 
 \[R=\frac{P_{ResNet}}{P_{EfficientNet}}.\] 
 Round only the final ratio. The parameter reduction of model B relative to model A is  \(100(1-P_B/P_A)\%\) ; it is a different quantity from the ratio. Neither calculation tells you how much peak GPU memory will change. 
 Fictional Practice 
 If two toy models have 9 million and 3 million parameters, their ratio is 3 and the smaller model has about 66.7% fewer parameters. Float32 parameter storage alone is count × 4 bytes. Gradients, buffers, AdamW moments, activations and temporary workspaces are additional allocations. 
 3. Why Depthwise Convolution Can Save Parameters 
 A standard  \(k\times k\)  convolution with  \(C_{in}\)  inputs and  \(C_{out}\)  outputs has  \(k^2C_{in}C_{out}\)  kernel weights. A depthwise convolution followed by a pointwise projection has: 
 \[k^2C_{in}+C_{in}C_{out}.\] 
 For a toy  \(3\times3\)  layer from 8 to 16 channels, these counts are 1152 and 200. This simplified comparison excludes biases and normalization. 
 EfficientNet's MBConv blocks additionally include channel expansion, squeeze-and-excitation and projection. Count the complete block to estimate actual savings. Expanded intermediate activations may still be large. ResNet's residual additions aid optimization; they do not by themselves determine the full model's memory footprint. 
 4. Measure GPU Memory under a Defined Workload 
 For Q9 report  training peak allocated CUDA memory  at batch size 16, native resolution and float32. Run each model in a fresh process on the same GPU. Initialize its optimizer, warm up two full optimizer steps (including AdamW state creation), synchronize, reset peak statistics, and measure one more complete step: 
 # After warm-up steps, before the measured zero_grad/forward/backward/step:
torch.cuda.synchronize()
torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
# Run a complete optimizer step here with the fixed batch/protocol.
torch.cuda.synchronize()
peak_mib = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**20 
 Report allocated memory rather than reserved caching-allocator memory, and use the same measurement boundaries for both models. If either model runs out of memory, report that outcome; do not silently reduce its batch size. On a CPU-only runtime report  not_measured  for CUDA memory. 
 Inference is a separate workload: no gradients or AdamW state, usually a deployment-specific batch size and dtype. A training memory measurement alone is insufficient to certify suitability for an edge device. Measure inference memory and latency on the target device before making that claim. 
 5. Compare Scores without a Preset Winner 
 Use  Guide 8's official metric . Record both epoch-5 scores and their signed difference. For this assessment, “competitive” means the EfficientNet score is no more than 0.01 below the ResNet score; this is a declared comparison tolerance, not an expected result. A higher score also meets that definition. 
 A smaller model can generalize well, but it can also underfit or need a different training schedule. Five epochs do not establish a model's eventual best performance. Repeat seeds or train longer only as a separately labeled follow-up. 
 
 Practice: Model A has fewer weights but a larger activation tensor. Which has lower peak VRAM? 
 The parameter counts alone are insufficient. Measure the complete workload; activations, temporary workspaces, gradients and optimizer state can change the ranking.
